title: Do it to all of them
briefing: ~/reports holds three monthly reports: jan.txt, feb.txt, mar.txt. They've
been signed off, so archive each one by renaming it to add a .done suffix
Doing it by hand is three commands. A loop does it in one — and in one
hundred the same way. That's what `for` is for.
tips: `for f in *.txt; do ... ; done` runs the body once per matching file, with $f set to each.
objective: In ~/reports, rename every .txt file to add a .done suffix (so jan.txt becomes jan.txt.done, and no .txt file is left).
expert_objective: Archive every .txt in ~/reports to .txt.done with one loop.
hints: A for loop walks a list: `for f in *.txt; do ...; done`. Each time, $f is one filename.
`cd ~/reports`, then `for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "$f.done"; done`.
solution:
cd ~/reports
for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "$f.done"; done
explanation: A `for` loop repeats a command for every item in a list — here every file matching *.txt. The loop variable ($f) takes each value in turn. Learn this and batch work stops being tedious: the same loop handles three files or three thousand.
